title: Why would ZGC — designed for sub-millisecond pauses — still produce a huge periodic latency spike (an ALLOCATION STALL: the allocation rate outpaces concurrent reclamation so threads are parked until memory frees), how does `ZUncommit` giving heap back to the OS during quiet periods worsen a bursty workload (page faults + zeroing when memory is reclaimed), and how do you fix it (`-Xms == -Xmx` to disable uncommit, `-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch` to fault in all pages at startup, and `-XX:+ZGenerational` to collect the young gen frequently)?
shortTitle: Why ZGC can still show a huge periodic latency spike — the allocation stall — how ZUncommit worsens bursty workloads, and how to fix it

s1_definition.profdef: An allocation stall in ZGC happens when the application's allocation rate outpaces ZGC's concurrent reclamation, so there is no free memory to satisfy a new allocation; the allocating thread is parked until the collector frees space. This is not the normal sub-millisecond GC pause — it is the application being blocked waiting for memory, and it shows up as a large periodic latency spike. ZUncommit, which returns unused heap to the operating system during quiet periods, can make a bursty workload worse because the next burst must re-commit memory, triggering page faults and zeroing before the pages are usable.
s1_definition.analogy: The renovation crew (ZGC) normally works in the background without stopping customers. But if a sudden rush of customers (a burst) fills every desk faster than the crew can clear old ones, a new customer has nowhere to sit and must wait at the door until a desk opens — that waiting-at-the-door is an allocation stall. Worse, if during a quiet hour the bank returned some desks to the landlord (ZUncommit), then when the rush hits it must first get those desks back, unlock them and clean them (page faults and zeroing) before anyone can sit — adding delay exactly when it is busiest.
s1_definition.oneliner: ZGC's pauses stay tiny, but if allocation outruns reclamation the app stalls waiting for memory, and ZUncommit makes bursts worse by forcing re-commit; fix it with fixed heap, pre-touch, and generational mode.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An allocation stall in ZGC happens when the application's allocation rate outpaces ZGC's concurrent reclamation, so there is no free memory to satisfy a new allocation; the allocating thread is parked until the collector frees space. This is not the normal sub-millisecond GC pause — it is the application being blocked waiting for memory, and it shows up as a large periodic latency spike. ZUncommit, which returns unused heap to the operating system during quiet periods, can make a bursty workload worse because the next burst must re-commit memory, triggering page faults and zeroing before the pages are usable.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The renovation crew (ZGC) normally works in the background without stopping customers. But if a sudden rush of customers (a burst) fills every desk faster than the crew can clear old ones, a new customer has nowhere to sit and must wait at the door until a desk opens — that waiting-at-the-door is an allocation stall. Worse, if during a quiet hour the bank returned some desks to the landlord (ZUncommit), then when the rush hits it must first get those desks back, unlock them and clean them (page faults and zeroing) before anyone can sit — adding delay exactly when it is busiest.

**One line to remember:** ZGC's pauses stay tiny, but if allocation outruns reclamation the app stalls waiting for memory, and ZUncommit makes bursts worse by forcing re-commit; fix it with fixed heap, pre-touch, and generational mode.

sections.s2_technical:
ZGC's famous sub-millisecond pause refers to the stop-the-world portion of a GC cycle. It does not promise the application never waits. If the application allocates faster than ZGC can concurrently reclaim and relocate, free memory runs out, and the only safe thing the JVM can do is park the allocating thread until the collector frees some space. This is an allocation stall, and from the outside it looks like a big latency spike that recurs under load — precisely the opposite of what people expect from ZGC.

Allocation stalls have a few common causes. The heap may simply be too small for the allocation rate, leaving no slack for the collector to work in. The allocation rate may be spiky, so a sudden burst exhausts the free space before the next concurrent cycle completes. Or in non-generational mode the collector wastes effort scanning the whole heap, reclaiming slowly relative to the churn.

ZUncommit is a feature where ZGC returns heap memory it is not currently using back to the operating system during quiet periods, which is friendly to multi-tenant hosts and containers because it lowers the resident footprint. The catch is that re-acquiring that memory is not free. When the next burst arrives and the JVM needs those pages again, the OS must map and zero them, which causes page faults and CPU-costly zeroing at exactly the wrong moment — during the burst. For a steady workload ZUncommit is fine; for a bursty one it adds latency spikes on top of the stall risk.

The fixes work together. Setting `-Xms` equal to `-Xmx` makes the heap a fixed size, which disables uncommit because there is no "unused committed heap" to give back; the JVM holds all its memory for its whole life. Adding `-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch` makes the JVM fault in and zero every heap page at startup rather than lazily on first use, so the first burst does not pay page-fault and zeroing costs — you move that cost to a slightly slower startup, which is a good trade for a latency-sensitive service. And `-XX:+ZGenerational` (default from Java 23) makes ZGC collect the young generation frequently and cheaply, so it reclaims the short-lived burst garbage fast and keeps enough free space ahead of the allocation rate, which is the structural fix for stalls. In addition, you give the heap enough headroom so the concurrent collector always has room to work.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's end-of-day settlement service is quiet most of the day, then at market close a huge burst of trades floods in. During the burst the service allocates far faster than usual. On ZGC with a growable heap it occasionally froze for hundreds of milliseconds right at the busiest moment. This is an allocation stall — allocation outran reclamation.

Problem 2 — Investigation showed the heap had shrunk during the quiet afternoon because ZUncommit returned pages to the OS, so when the close burst hit, the JVM had to re-commit and zero memory, adding page-fault latency on top of the stall. This is the ZUncommit-worsens-bursts problem.

Our mini-project is a runnable burst simulator: a long quiet phase with low allocation followed by a sudden high-allocation burst, logging allocation rate and GC behaviour so you can see the stall risk, plus the three-flag fix printed clearly. Classes are `SettlementBurstSimulator` (driver with quiet and burst phases), `TradeBatch` (the burst allocator), and `AllocationMeter` (tracks approximate allocation rate and logs it).
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
zgc-stall-demo/
├── pom.xml
├── run.sh
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/stall/
            ├── SettlementBurstSimulator.java   (main + demo classes)
            └── AllocationMeter.java
```

Configuration (JVM flags):

```bash
# zgc-stall-fix.conf — the three-part fix for allocation stalls on bursty load
-XX:+UseZGC
-Xms6g -Xmx6g            # equal → disables ZUncommit, no give-back/re-commit churn
-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch      # fault in & zero all pages at startup, not during the burst
# -XX:+ZGenerational     # Java 21/22 only; default from Java 23
-Xlog:gc*,gc+alloc=debug:file=gc.log:time,tags   # gc+alloc shows stalls
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn -q clean package

# BAD: growable heap on bursty load — ZUncommit + stall risk
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms512m -Xmx6g \
     -Xlog:gc+alloc=debug:file=gc-bad.log:time,tags \
     -cp target/zgc-stall-demo-1.0.0.jar com.bank.jvm.stall.SettlementBurstSimulator

# GOOD: the three-part fix
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms6g -Xmx6g -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch \
     -Xlog:gc+alloc=debug:file=gc-good.log:time,tags \
     -cp target/zgc-stall-demo-1.0.0.jar com.bank.jvm.stall.SettlementBurstSimulator

# Count allocation stalls in each run (should be >0 in bad, 0 in good)
grep -i "Allocation Stall" gc-bad.log  | wc -l
grep -i "Allocation Stall" gc-good.log | wc -l
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a three-second quiet phase allocating small `TradeBatch` objects, then a burst of four hundred large `TradeBatch` objects, run under ZGC.

Step 1. During the quiet phase the allocation rate is low. ZGC's concurrent cycles easily keep ahead, and with a growable heap the JVM may even uncommit pages back to the OS because the heap looks over-provisioned.

Step 2. The burst begins. The loop allocates large batches rapidly. The allocation rate recorded by `AllocationMeter` jumps sharply — this is the moment of danger.

Step 3. On a growable heap that had uncommitted memory, the JVM now needs those pages back. The OS maps and zeroes them, causing page faults and zeroing CPU cost mid-burst. Meanwhile free space is scarce, so if allocation outruns concurrent reclamation, allocating threads are parked — an allocation stall — and latency spikes.

Step 4. With the fix applied, `-Xms` equals `-Xmx`, so the heap is fixed and ZUncommit never gave pages away; there is nothing to re-commit. All pages were pre-touched at startup, so no page faults happen during the burst.

Step 5. Generational ZGC collects the young generation frequently, so the short-lived burst batches that do not survive are reclaimed quickly, keeping free space ahead of the allocation rate. The few retained survivors go to the old generation without disturbing young-collection speed.

Step 6. The gc.log confirms the outcome: the bad run shows "Allocation Stall" lines during the burst, while the good run shows none, and the meter shows the same high allocation rate handled without stalling.

sections.s6_takeaway:
ZGC's sub-millisecond guarantee is about the stop-the-world portion of a collection, not a promise that the application never waits. If the application allocates faster than ZGC can concurrently reclaim and relocate, free memory runs out and the JVM has no choice but to park the allocating thread until space is freed. That is an allocation stall, and it appears as a large, recurring latency spike under load, which surprises people because it is the opposite of what ZGC is known for. The root cause is always that allocation outran reclamation, usually from a heap that is too small for the rate, a spiky bursty workload, or the old non-generational mode reclaiming too slowly.

ZUncommit makes a bursty workload worse. It returns unused heap to the operating system during quiet periods to keep the footprint small, which is fine for steady load. But when the next burst arrives the JVM must re-acquire those pages, and the OS maps and zeroes them, causing page faults and zeroing cost at exactly the busiest moment, stacking extra latency on top of the stall risk.

The fix is three things working together. I set minimum heap equal to maximum heap so the heap size is fixed, which disables uncommit entirely because there is no unused committed heap to give back. I add AlwaysPreTouch so the JVM faults in and zeroes every page at startup, paying that cost once during a slightly slower boot instead of during a live burst. And I use generational ZGC, the default from Java 23, so the young generation is collected frequently and cheaply and free space stays ahead of the allocation rate, which is the structural cure. At National Bank of India our end-of-day settlement service stalled for hundreds of milliseconds right at market close; fixing the heap, pre-touching, and running generationally eliminated the stalls, and I proved it by alerting on the allocation-stall count in the gc-plus-alloc log against the trade-volume curve.
